lines: Riley Chen
+1 (555) 010-7731 | riley.chen@example.com | example.com/in/riley-chen
EDUCATION
Northfield School of Management | MBA | Metro City, USA | Sep 2023 - Jun 2025
Lakeview University | B.A. in Economics | Lake City, USA | Sep 2014 - Jun 2018
EXPERIENCE
Coastal Marine Services | Diesel Mechanic | Lake City, USA | Jul 2025 - Present
- Rebuilt diesel engines and gearboxes for a fleet of 14 commercial fishing vessels, keeping dry-dock time under 5 days per job.
- Maintained hydraulic winch systems and logged service records for the harbor authority's annual inspections.
Crestline Logistics | Operations Analyst | Lake City, USA | Jul 2018 - Aug 2023
- Owned the weekly carrier scorecards for the regional managers and the monthly review meeting that discussed them.
- Cut warehouse pick errors 30% at two sites by redesigning slotting rules with the floor supervisors and retraining 45 pickers on the new layout.
- Ran the quarterly S&OP review across sales, finance and operations for 12 consecutive quarters, introducing a consensus forecast that cut forecast error from 18% to 11%.

- Led the rollout of a route-planning tool to 3 depots while rewriting the standard operating procedures, running driver training and taking over vendor negotiations for the telematics contract, which saved 1,800 driver hours a year across the region.
Harbor Payments | Associate Product Manager Intern | Metro City, USA | Jun 2024 - Aug 2024
- Redesigned merchant onboarding around a single verification step, cutting median time to first payment from 9 days to 4 across 2,300 new merchants in the pilot region.
- Lifted checkout conversion from 61% to 66% by testing a one-page flow against the three-step flow across 40,000 sessions, then shipping it to all merchants.
- Prioritized the dispute roadmap with RICE, scoring Reach as the number of support tickets each feature would close.
- After interviewing 25 merchants, mapping chargeback reasons, sizing the loss by segment and drafting a business case with finance, set the next quarter's roadmap priority.
- Ran the checkout A/B test with randomization by session and reported the 5-point conversion lift as the effect on merchants' customers.
- Presented the onboarding results and a follow-up roadmap to the payments leadership team, who funded the rollout to two more regions.
PROJECTS
Campus Food Rescue App | Product Lead | Student Venture | Oct 2023 - Present
- Launched a surplus-food pickup app to 3,100 students with two dining halls, redistributing 9 tonnes of food that would have been thrown away in its first year.
- Raised weekly active users from 400 to 1,150, a 150% increase, by adding pickup reminders chosen after 60 user interviews.
- Raised the pickup-slot fill rate by 20% across two dining halls, from 75% to 95%, by setting up a volunteer shift system.
MBA Consulting Practicum | Team Lead | Regional Hospital Network | Jan 2024 - May 2024
- Sized a $2.4M annual saving from consolidating outpatient scheduling across 4 clinics; the client funded a pilot based on the model.
- Patient intake at 4 clinics was mapped and the intake form was shortened, with the changes adopted by front-desk staff.
- Presented the final recommendation to the hospital COO and clinic directors, who approved a 90-day scheduling pilot at two clinics.
SKILLS
Product: roadmapping, A/B testing, user interviews, requirements writing
Tools: Jira, Amplitude, Excel

items.says: The experience order is not newest-first and makes the post-MBA career direction appear to move backward.
items.because: Crestline appears above the more recent Harbor internship, while Coastal is presented first after Education.

items.says: Projects should appear before Education if product management is the target.
items.because: The product internship and student product work are stronger evidence of the target direction than the academic history.

items.says: The two checkout-testing bullets repeat the same A/B test and five-point improvement.
items.because: The repetition uses space, reads like a task list, and forces the reader to reconcile two descriptions of one result.

items.says: The two dispute-roadmap bullets repeat the same prioritization work.
items.because: The duplication fragments one product decision across its research, sizing, method, and outcome.

items.says: The practicum repeats the scheduling-pilot approval in two bullets.
items.because: The repetition spends space without adding evidence.

items.says: The dry-dock result has no comparison showing whether under five days was an improvement, a standard, or the normal turnaround.
items.because: The reader cannot judge the result's significance without a prior average, target, or reduction.

items.says: “Maintained” does not show the technical work performed on the hydraulic winch systems.
items.because: It could mean inspection, troubleshooting, repair, adjustment, or replacement, so the hands-on skill is unclear.

items.says: The service-record phrase gives no operational result or inspection outcome.
items.because: It shows activity but not whether operations or inspection readiness improved.

items.says: The carrier-scorecard bullet gives no result.
items.because: It does not show whether the work improved carrier performance, service, cost, or decisions.

items.says: The carrier-scorecard bullet gives no clear operating mechanism.
items.because: “Owned” and “discussed them” make the contribution look like administration rather than analysis and operational follow-through.

items.says: The S&OP acronym is unexplained jargon.
items.because: Readers outside supply-chain planning may not know it means sales and operations planning.

items.says: The forecast-error improvement appears too late in the bullet.
items.because: A scanner may focus on the recurring review rather than the 18%-to-11% result.

items.says: The route-planning bullet buries the 1,800-hour result after too many actions.
items.because: A scanning reader may miss the strongest evidence.

items.says: The 1,800-hour saving has no comparison point.
items.because: Without prior hours, a percentage reduction, or a cost equivalent, its scale is difficult to interpret.

items.says: “Taking over vendor negotiations” sounds like a handoff rather than an accomplishment.
items.because: The wording makes that responsibility appear less achievement-oriented.

items.says: The line implies that 40,000 sessions alone justified rollout to all merchants.
items.because: Session volume does not establish randomization, statistical reliability, guardrail performance, or representativeness of all merchants.

items.says: “Shipping it” has an ambiguous antecedent.
items.because: The reader may not know whether “it” means the one-page flow or the experiment.

items.says: The line incorrectly defines RICE Reach as raw support-ticket volume rather than unique affected users, customers, or accounts over a defined period.
items.because: Repeat reports can count the same user more than once and do not establish affected-user reach.

items.says: The RICE bullet gives no resulting roadmap change.
items.because: It shows familiarity with a framework rather than the decision it produced.

items.says: The RICE bullet gives no comparison from the scoring.
items.because: The reader cannot tell why one feature ranked ahead of another.

items.says: “Sizing the loss by segment” gives no loss estimate.
items.because: The reader cannot see what the analysis established.

items.says: “Sizing the loss by segment” gives no segment comparison.
items.because: The reader cannot see why one segment mattered more.

items.says: “Sizing the loss” uses internal jargon.
items.because: Readers outside payments or finance may find the bullet less immediately clear.

items.says: The bullet does not identify the roadmap priority selected.
items.because: The reader cannot tell which problem the next quarter would address.

items.says: The bullet does not state the selected priority's expected value.
items.because: The reader cannot tell what the research and business case were expected to change.

items.says: The process list buries the roadmap decision under four research and business-case activities.
items.because: A scanning reader may miss the product outcome, leaving the bullet focused on activity rather than judgment.

items.says: The line calls the 61%-to-66% movement a five-point lift instead of a five-percentage-point lift.
items.because: The metric moved by five percentage points, not 5 percent.

items.says: The session-level experiment is incorrectly reported as an effect on merchants' customers.
items.because: Session randomization does not automatically support customer-level inference when customers may have repeat sessions or see both variants.

items.says: The funding bullet does not identify which onboarding result supported the rollout decision.
items.because: The reader cannot connect the funding to a specific measured improvement.

items.says: The “who funded” construction emphasizes the leadership team instead of what the presentation secured.
items.because: It makes the candidate's role in obtaining approval less clear.

items.says: The app's launch scope across two dining halls is ambiguous.
items.because: “With two dining halls” can appear to modify the launch rather than the app's operating scope.

items.says: The claim that all nine tonnes would otherwise have been thrown away is unsupported.
items.because: Recording food collected through the app does not prove the avoided-waste counterfactual.

items.says: The launch bullet does not show the product or operating method that produced the result.
items.because: The reader cannot tell what product-lead contribution made the redistribution possible.

items.says: The stated 150% increase is arithmetically wrong; growth from 400 to 1,150 is 187.5%.
items.because: A 150% increase from 400 would reach 1,000.

items.says: The rise in weekly active users is attributed entirely to pickup reminders without evidence that the reminders caused it.
items.because: The interviews do not rule out seasonality, promotion, or another change as a contributor.

items.says: “Chosen after 60 user interviews” does not clearly explain what the interviews informed.
items.because: The reader cannot tell whether they informed the reminder concept, content, timing, or another feature detail.

items.says: The line incorrectly describes the change from 75% to 95% as a 20% increase rather than a 20-percentage-point increase.
items.because: The relative increase is approximately 26.7%, while the endpoints differ by 20 percentage points.

items.says: The volunteer-shift method is too generic to show how it improved pickup-slot fill.
items.because: The reader cannot see what the shift system changed operationally.

items.says: The $2.4M annual-saving estimate lacks a cost or operating baseline.
items.because: The reader cannot quickly tell how the figure was calculated or what current cost it represents.

items.says: “Based on the model” is vague about how the client used the analysis.
items.because: The reader cannot tell whether the model supported approval, prioritization, design, or another decision.

items.says: The intake-process bullet gives no resulting improvement.
items.because: Staff adoption proves acceptance, not whether the change reduced effort, time, errors, or patient friction.

items.says: The bullet does not quantify how much the intake form was shortened.
items.because: Without a before-and-after measure, the reader cannot judge whether the improvement was material.

items.says: The passive wording hides the candidate's contribution.
items.because: It does not actively identify what the candidate changed.

items.says: “Final recommendation” is generic and does not identify the analysis or subject behind it.
items.because: The reader sees senior-stakeholder exposure but not the consulting skill supporting the recommendation.
